assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks turned a clever proposal (magic-wavelength trapping) into the most precise measurement devices ever built, with fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. They open new observation channels: relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and dark-matter searches, and a path to redefining the second. This is the kind of instrument that changes what can be measured.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and demonstrated the first strontium lattice clock; Ye's group drove the record-precision implementations and the many-body and clock-comparison work. The two-name credit is clean. Other groups (e.g. Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley) contributed, but the conceptual and early-demonstration core is well covered.
assessment.maturity: Independently confirmed by many labs worldwide with repeated record improvements and cross-comparisons; the interpretation is stable and the field is mature. The redefinition of the SI second is still pending, but the science does not depend on it. Timing is good.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes (Hall, Hansch, Wineland) could be read as dilution of novelty.
Whether Ye's group contributions are best credited jointly with Katori or whether Lemonde or Ludlow deserve consideration is a matter for debate.
I am relying on memory for the precise record uncertainty figures and have not verified them here.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED provides the architecture behind modern superconducting quantum processors: strong coupling of a superconducting qubit to a microwave resonator, dispersive readout and the transmon. It is an experimental platform with a very large downstream impact on quantum information and quantum sensing.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin and Schoelkopf wrote the 2004 proposal and Wallraff et al. gave the first strong-coupling demonstration, with Schoelkopf's Yale group developing the transmon and circuit-QED readout. With four names credited a three-person prize forces a hard choice. I propose Schoelkopf, Wallraff and Girvin as the experimental and conceptual core, while acknowledging Blais's theoretical role.
assessment.maturity: Strong, independent, long-running confirmation across many groups and industrial platforms; the physics is firmly established. Recognition is timely, though the 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits touches the same community and may affect timing.
uncertainties: The relation to the most recent superconducting-circuit prize may argue for waiting.
Excluding Blais, or Devoret-school contributors to the transmon, is contentious.
Exact credit between proposal and first demonstration should be checked against the original papers.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of single NV centres created a room-temperature solid-state quantum sensor with nanoscale magnetic, electric and thermal sensitivity, applied in biology, materials and geophysics. This is a new measurement technique, demonstrated experimentally and widely used, which is the direction I value.
assessment.attribution: Gruber and Wrachtrup (1997) showed optical detection of single NV spins; Jelezko and Wrachtrup demonstrated coherent control and spin readout; Lukin's group extended this to nanoscale magnetometry, quantum registers and sensing. The three-name configuration is sensible, though other groups (Awschalom, Hanson, Walsworth, Budker) also made major contributions.
assessment.maturity: Highly reproducible and widely adopted in many labs; sensing applications are increasingly mature, with commercialisation emerging. The foundational result is more than two decades old, so timing is fair.
uncertainties: Overlap in credit with B040 (spin-photon interfaces) and other diamond-spin work.
Several equally deserving contributors (e.g. Awschalom, Hanson) are left out of any three-person split.
Whether sensing applications or the quantum-information results should be foregrounded is unresolved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry underlies precision measurements of gravity, the gravity gradient, rotation and the fine-structure constant, with proposals for gravitational-wave and dark-matter detection. It is a core measurement technology in cold-atom physics, matching my interest in experiment-driven precision.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard's group demonstrated the first atom interferometers with material gratings and Bordé proposed the Ramsey-Bordé interferometer geometry, while Kasevich (with Chu) produced the first precision atom-light-pulse gravimeter. Chu's contribution is not in the credited names, so credit is fragmentary and somewhat awkward given his 1997 prize. I propose the three credited names.
assessment.maturity: Demonstrated and replicated by many groups, with field-deployed gravimeters; large-scale fundamental-physics applications (gravitational-wave detection, equivalence-principle tests) are still being developed. The field is mature in methods, but its biggest payoffs remain ahead.
uncertainties: Attribution is unclear without Chu and given Ramsey-Bordé versus light-pulse lineages.
The decisive science may still be to come, so recognition could be premature.
I cannot verify the exact priority claims from memory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ti:sapphire gain media and Kerr-lens or semiconductor-saturable-absorber mode-locking made practical, compact, tunable femtosecond lasers. They enabled ultrafast spectroscopy, frequency combs and attosecond science, much of which has been recognised separately. The enabling-instrument impact is clear and broad.
assessment.attribution: Moulton demonstrated Ti:sapphire as a tunable laser medium; Sibbett's group demonstrated Kerr-lens mode-locking; Keller developed SESAM passive mode-locking. The names map to separate decisive inventions, which supports a three-way prize, though other Kerr-lens contributors (e.g. Spence, Kean) are omitted.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature and ubiquitous, with decades of confirmation and use. This is not premature; the risk is that it is late and partly absorbed by earlier prizes on combs, CPA and attosecond pulses.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2005 and 2018 prizes may lower priority.
Credit across Ti:sapphire, Kerr-lens and SESAM involves distinct inventions that may not form one discovery.
Priority for Kerr-lens mode-locking (Sibbett's group versus Spence) should be verified.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices became a controllable quantum simulator: the superfluid-Mott transition, quantum gas microscopes with single-site resolution, and engineered Hubbard models. It opens a way to observe many-body physics at the microscopic level, which is attractive from a measurement standpoint.
assessment.attribution: Jaksch, Zoller and co-authors proposed the Bose-Hubbard realisation; Greiner, Bloch and Hänsch demonstrated the Mott transition; Greiner and Bloch developed quantum gas microscopes. Five names are credited, so I propose the three that best represent theory, first demonstration and single-site imaging, noting that Dalibard and Cirac are also important.
assessment.maturity: Many independent groups have reproduced and extended the results; the platform is mature, though the headline goal of solving open problems such as the Fermi-Hubbard phase diagram is still developing.
uncertainties: Five credited names do not fit a prize cleanly and the omissions are contentious.
Overlaps with B023, B033 and B041 for Zoller and Cirac complicate a joint configuration.
Whether quantum simulation has yet delivered a decisive new physical insight remains open.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Producing and controlling ultracold molecules enables precision tests of fundamental symmetries (the electron EDM), ultracold chemistry and new quantum platforms. Experimentally these are difficult achievements with real measurement payoffs, notably the ACME electron EDM bounds.
assessment.attribution: DeMille and Doyle pioneered molecule cooling and trapping and the ACME EDM experiments, while Ye contributed KRb ultracold molecules and precision spectroscopy; the group of Ni and Jin (Jin deceased) is relevant but Jin is not credited. Bundling several distinct achievements makes this a compound discovery whose parts may merit different recognition.
assessment.maturity: Progress is rapid and confirmed by several groups (laser-cooled molecules, tweezer arrays), but the signature scientific outcomes, such as a new EDM limit or controlled chemistry, are still evolving; some elements may be premature.
uncertainties: Compound credit across molecule production, cooling and EDM experiments.
Jin's contributions cannot be recognised posthumously, which complicates attribution.
Maturity of the application results is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution is a conceptually clean application of quantum mechanics to cryptography, linking foundations (Bell tests, entanglement) with technology. It has been demonstrated over fibre and satellite links and commercialised, though the practical impact is still modest.
assessment.attribution: BB84 by Bennett and Brassard and E91 by Ekert are the two foundational protocols, so the three-name credit is natural and fits a prize. Wiesner's earlier conjugate-coding idea and Bennett's later work create a minor priority question.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed by many experiments, with the foundations (Bell tests) already recognised in 2022. Recognition is mature and plausible, but the real-world impact of QKD relative to post-quantum cryptography is debated.
uncertainties: Practical security and deployment limits of real QKD systems.
Overlap with the 2022 prize for entanglement and Bell tests.
Wiesner's priority is a question I cannot resolve from memory.
